records.title: From chronic disease burden to cognitive decline: a systematic review of multimorbidity in older adults
records.abstract: Multimorbidity is common in older adults and has been associated with adverse cognitive outcomes. However, findings remain heterogeneous because of differences in multimorbidity definitions, cognitive measures, and study designs. This review aimed to synthesize evidence on the association between multimorbidity and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years.  Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and gray literature sources were searched up to August 2026. Observational studies examining multimorbidity, defined as ≥ 2 chronic conditions, and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years were included. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists, and findings were synthesized narratively.  Seventeen studies met the eligibility criteria. Overall, greater multimorbidity burden was generally associated with poorer cognitive outcomes, while several specific multimorbidity patterns, particularly cardiometabolic and cardiovascular patterns, were associated with cognitive impairment, cognitive decline, or dementia. However, some studies reported null or domain-specific associations. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across multimorbidity definitions, cognitive assessments, study designs, populations, and confounding adjustment.  Multimorbidity may be associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in older adults, but the strength and consistency of the evidence vary across studies. Interpretation is limited by methodological heterogeneity, potential risk of bias, and the observational nature of the evidence. More standardized prospective studies are needed to clarify these associations.

records.title: Probable sarcopenia, depressive symptoms, and nutritional status as independent predictors of dysphagia risk in community-dwelling older adults
records.abstract: Dysphagia is a critical geriatric syndrome associated with an increased risk of aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and mortality in older adults. The aim of this study was to evaluate the associations between Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) parameters and dysphagia risk (Eating Assessment Tool-10 (EAT-10) ≥ 3) in community-dwelling older adults.  This cross-sectional study included 468 community-dwelling older adults presenting to a geriatric outpatient clinic. Participants with severe cognitive impairment, Parkinson’s disease, those residing in a nursing home, and those with an acute medical condition were excluded from the study. Dysphagia risk was assessed using the EAT-10; probable sarcopenia was defined according to the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2019 (EWGSOP2) criteria; depressive symptoms were evaluated with the Geriatric Depression Scale-15 (GDS-15); and nutritional status was assessed using the Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form (MNA-SF). Independent risk factors were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.  In the final multivariate regression model, the presence of probable sarcopenia (OR = 2.654, 95% CI: 1.184–5.947, p = 0.018) and higher GDS-15 scores (OR = 1.155, 95% CI: 1.063–1.255, p = 0.001) were independently and significantly associated with dysphagia risk. In contrast, a one-point increase in the MNA-SF score (indicating better nutritional status), when treated as a continuous variable, was an independent protective factor against dysphagia risk (OR = 0.684, 95% CI: 0.521–0.897, p = 0.006).  In community-dwelling older adults, probable sarcopenia and depressive symptoms significantly increase the dysphagia risk, whereas good nutritional status plays a protective role. Prior to the development of dysphagia and its associated complications, optimizing muscle strength, mood, and nutritional status in outpatient settings is of importance for maintaining swallowing safety.

records.title: Navigating a new era of disease-modifying therapy: experiences, treatment preferences, and unmet expectations of family caregivers of Alzheimer’s patients receiving lecanemab in China
records.abstract: Introduction As one of the newest disease-modifying therapies for early Alzheimer’s disease, lecanemab has attracted widespread research interest in various clinical settings around the world. However, there is currently insufficient understanding of patients’ and family caregivers’ real-world treatment experiences.  This study employed an exploratory qualitative research design and conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with family caregivers of patients with early AD who are currently receiving lecanemab treatment.  Three themes emerged: (1) Experiences and Attitudes Toward Lecanemab Treatment; (2) The Multiple Practical Challenges of Treatment Costs, Informed Decision-Making, and Efficacy Assessment; (3) Strategies for Future Improvements. Discussion Given the current state of healthcare in China, families of Alzheimer’s patients still have high hopes for lecanemab treatment. Although some patients report that it has slowed the rate of cognitive decline, factors such as high costs and significant side effects make treatment decisions extremely complex. Impact These findings provide valuable real-world insights into the use of Lecanemab in Chinese Alzheimer’s patients, thereby informing and improving the design of future clinical studies. Reporting method This study adhered to the COREQ guideline. Public contributions No paper or public contribution. Clinical trial number not applicable.

records.title: Motivations, Barriers, and the Potential of AI in Physical Activity Apps for US Older Adults: Interview Study
records.abstract: The older adult population is increasing rapidly and experiences a multitude of chronic conditions affecting quality of life. Physical activity and reduced sedentary behavior reduce adverse health conditions and help preserve functional independence and cognitive abilities, but the older adult age group has much lower levels of physical activity than recommended compared with other population demographics.  The study aimed to understand older adults’ motivations toward health and physical activity and the role of technology in achieving their health and physical activity goals and to explore the attitudes toward the use of generative AI in health apps.  This study was qualitative and based on hour-long interviews with 20 older adults living in the United States. To elicit specific design preferences, participants were presented with visual probes of AI-generated avatars. The interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis, and the coding process drew on reflexive and grounded theory techniques.  Older adults primarily wished to maintain functional independence, both physical and cognitive, prioritizing baseline maintenance rather than continuous optimization. They reported satisfaction with levels of physical activity, adjusting them to chronic conditions and injuries. They were active through everyday functions of living as well as structured exercise programs with many participants using wearable devices and smartphones to help monitor their activity. They reported being motivated by social accountability and gamification, although some found the latter condescending or anxiety-inducing. Accessibility issues were mentioned frequently, including problems with touchscreens, limited viewing, difficulty navigating interfaces with clutter, complex multitouch processes for undertaking actions, and steep learning curves. Computers were preferred for certain tasks over mobile phones due to easier viewability, keyboard access, and greater security features. Personalization was highly desired in health apps. There was a willingness to use more health technology, including generative AI, and they were willing to consider AI in both motivational and informational roles in apps as long as it was personalized. AI embodiment preferences varied widely but with an emphasis on relatability. However, there was marked skepticism toward data privacy, concerns about the loss of independence and self-efficacy, and doubts about AI’s accuracy.  Older adults are primarily motivated by sustaining functional independence, although accessibility barriers in current health apps remain. Participants were open to AI for physical activity support, but expectations varied. They viewed AI as a passive “tool,” a directive “coach,” or a relational “companion.” Considerable variation in preferences for gamification and visual design suggested that future apps require greater modularity. As skepticism over data privacy and AI accuracy remains high, greater transparency and explainability might be needed to engender trust.

records.title: Osteoporosis in the Oldest Old - From Diagnosis to Treatment: A Narrative Review
records.abstract: Osteoporosis and fragility fractures are major causes of disability, loss of independence, institutionalization, and mortality in the oldest old. Despite their exceptionally high fracture risk, adults aged ≥80 years remain underrepresented in randomized controlled trials. Diagnosis and treatment are complicated by the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, sarcopenia, frailty, multimorbidity, cognitive and functional impairment, and competing mortality. Summary: This narrative review discusses the diagnosis, fracture-risk assessment, non-pharmacological management, and pharmacological treatment of osteoporosis in the oldest old. Bone mineral density (BMD) remains central to osteoporosis diagnosis but incompletely characterizes fracture risk at advanced age. Previous and particularly recent fractures, prevalent vertebral fractures, falls, physical performance, nutritional status, and frailty provide complementary information. Interpretation of the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool FRAX® requires particular consideration in the oldest old because competing mortality may cause 10-year fracture probabilities to plateau or decline despite increasing age-specific fracture incidence; FRAXplus® incorporates additional risk modifiers, including falls and the number and recency of previous fractures. Non-pharmacological interventions addressing nutrition, muscle function, balance, and falls complement bone-directed pharmacotherapy. Available evidence does not indicate that chronological age itself attenuates the efficacy of osteoporosis pharmacotherapy, although direct randomized fracture-endpoint evidence in adults aged ≥80 years remains limited. Risedronate and, historically, strontium ranelate provide some of the clearest fracture data specifically in this age group, whereas evidence for most other therapies derives from older-subgroup analyses, skeletal efficacy studies, observational data, or extrapolation from pivotal trials. At advanced age, renal function, cognition, mobility, adherence, caregiver support, and continuity of care increasingly influence the translation of efficacy into clinical effectiveness. Key Messages: Fracture risk in the oldest old reflects the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, frailty, sarcopenia, and functional reserve. Available evidence supports preservation of pharmacological antifracture efficacy with advancing age, but direct evidence in octogenarians and particularly nonagenarians remains scarce. Treatment feasibility and continuity of care become increasingly relevant at advanced age. Greater representation of the oldest old in clinical trials is needed, with particular attention to fracture outcomes, treatment sequencing, time to benefit, and outcomes relevant to independence and quality of life.

records.title: Sources of enjoyment in life and frailty among community-dwelling older adults: cross-sectional and longitudinal associations
records.abstract: Although greater life enjoyment is associated with a lower risk of frailty, little is known about the association between sources of life enjoyment and frailty. This study investigated the associations between the variety and types of sources of enjoyment in life (“enjoyment sources”) and frailty among community-dwelling older adults.  Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted using data from a community-based cohort study in Japan. In 2020, questionnaires were mailed to 4,996 randomly selected adults aged ≥65 years, and 2,764 responded. Follow-up questionnaires were sent to 1,635 consenting participants in 2023, with 904 responses obtained. Frailty was assessed using a 5-item self-report questionnaire at baseline and follow-up. Enjoyment sources were assessed through yes/no and open-ended questions at baseline and categorized using content analysis. The number of identified categories was counted, and participants were classified into no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups.  The cross-sectional analysis included 2,361 participants, and the prevalence of frailty was 26.6%, 16.7%, and 11.3% in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. Cross-sectional analyses showed that a greater variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of both prefrailty and frailty. In the 3-year longitudinal analysis, 688 participants were included. Among them, incident frailty occurred in 20.2%, 11.1%, and 10.0% of participants in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. The variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of incident frailty in both crude and basic adjusted models. The odds ratios for the single-source and multiple-source groups were similar. Exploratory analysis of the 10 most frequently reported enjoyment sources showed that books, sports, friends, foods, and singing/playing musical instruments showed inverse trends with frailty, whereas media consumption showed a positive trend with frailty in unadjusted cross-sectional trend tests. Discussion Having one or more enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of frailty among community-dwelling older adults in both cross-sectional and 3-year longitudinal analyses. The exploratory analysis also suggested that the associations between specific types of enjoyment sources and frailty may differ. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

records.title: Comparative evaluation of COVID-19 public health interventions and management in older populations: a scoping review and swot analysis of Cameroon and the United States
records.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disproportionately affected older adults (aged 65 years and older) due to age-related physiological vulnerabilities and forced social isolation. This study systematically evaluates the public health response and management strategies executed for older populations across two highly contrasting macroeconomic and governance structures: Cameroon, a Lower-Middle Income Country (LMIC), and the United States, a High-Income Country (HIC).  A scoping review and structured SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) analysis were conducted in strict accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. We systematically queried PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and African Journals Online (AJOL) for peer-reviewed literature, legal acts, and official institutional frameworks published between January 2020 and February 2026.  Twenty-two unique sources met all predefined inclusion criteria. Cameroon’s operational response drew heavily from highly decentralized, resilient community/kinship networks and immediate, government-mandated financial cushions, such as a 20% expansion in state pensions. However, these baseline mitigation efforts were severely restricted by deep structural healthcare weaknesses, a 73% fear-driven clinical avoidance rate, extreme diagnostic deficits (10.02 tests per 1,000 population), and resource constraints inside active conflict zones. Conversely, the United States leveraged massive technological capital, real-time molecular surveillance networks, and rapid mRNA vaccine rollouts that effectively averted an estimated 92% of potential deaths among older adults’ post-implementation, alongside a massive expansion of telehealth serving 59% of isolated seniors. Nevertheless, the United States response suffered from profound, catastrophic infection control failures within long-term care facilities, intense socio-political policy polarization and deep-seated institutionalized racial health inequities.  Future global pandemic preparedness frameworks must systematically integrate targeted “healthy aging” strategies directly into statutory national health policy architectures. This study demonstrates that isolated country analyses mask systemic vulnerabilities: HICs fail due to decentralization and polarization despite high GDP, while LMICs can innovate social resilience but remain strictly bottle-necked by material supply chains. Global preparedness metrics must abandon static spending indices in favor of structural equity and operational flexibility frameworks. Trial Registration Clinical trial number: not applicable.

records.title: Perceptions of Dementia Prevention on YouTube: A Thematic Analysis of Viewer Comments
records.abstract: Dementia prevention is receiving increasing attention considering the surge in number of dementia incidence worldwide. Although there are modifiable risk factors, the public remains largely unaware of dementia prevention. Many individuals turn to online platforms such as YouTube for health-related information, where content can shape beliefs, attitudes, and decision-making. However, little is known about how people interpret and discuss dementia prevention in these digital spaces. This study aimed to explore how dementia prevention is perceived by the public, as reflected in user generated comments posted on YouTube videos related to dementia prevention. A qualitative thematic analysis was conducted by examining comments from YouTube videos identified through Google Advanced Search. Twenty-six videos were selected based on predefined criteria, and comments were extracted and cleaned prior to analysis. Engagement metrics, including views, likes, and replies, were also examined to understand how users interacted with the content. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-step thematic approach. A total of 7314 comments were retrieved from 26 videos. Following data cleaning and removal of ineligible comments, 2034 comments were included for final analysis. Thematic analysis revealed three themes: (i) fear and perceived vulnerability to dementia; (ii) perceptions of dementia risk factors; and (iii) trust and credibility of dementia prevention information. These themes revealed fear, modifiable vs non-modifiable risk factors, and both public reliance on and distrust of scientific evidence. YouTube provides an important platform for public discussion about dementia prevention. Although it offers opportunities to increase awareness, viewer comments reflected inconsistent understandings and conflicting beliefs about dementia prevention, highlighting the need for clear, evidence-based communication to improve public understanding.

records.title: Healthy aging and quality of life in University of the Third Age students versus community peers: a cross-sectional study
records.abstract: This study aimed to compare healthy aging and quality of life levels between University of the Third Age (U3A) students and older adults not enrolled in the program and to examine the relationship between healthy aging and quality of life.  This descriptive, analytical, and cross-sectional study included 297 older adults aged 60 years and older (mean age: 68.51 ± 5.21 years): 146 U3A students and 151 older adults not enrolled in the program. Data were collected using the Participant Information Form, the Healthy Aging Instrument (HAI), and the Quality of Life Scale in Older People (CASP-19). Descriptive statistics, the Mann–Whitney U test, chi-square test, Spearman’s correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis were used.  U3A students had significantly higher HAI and CASP-19 total and subscale scores than older adults not enrolled in the program ( p p p  U3A students had higher healthy aging and quality of life scores than their peers who were not enrolled in the program, and these differences remained significant after adjustment for sociodemographic and health-related variables. A moderate positive correlation was also found between healthy aging and quality of life. These findings indicate that U3A programs may be considered within the scope of community-based healthy aging initiatives. However, causal inferences cannot be made because of the cross-sectional design.

records.title: Beyond BMI: The Role of Abdominal Obesity in Hypertension Risk Among Adults Aged 45 Years and Older in India
records.abstract: Hypertension is highly prevalent among adults aged 45 years and older in India, yet limited evidence exists on the combined associations of waist circumference (WC) and body mass index (BMI) with hypertension. This study examined their independent and joint associations with hypertension using Wave 1 (2017–18) of the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) among 59,658 adults aged 45 years and older. Hypertension was defined as measured blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations across combined WC–BMI categories. Overall hypertension prevalence was 31.3%. Individuals with normal BMI but large WC had higher odds of hypertension (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 1.37; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.19–1.58). Obese individuals with large WC had the highest odds (AOR = 1.77; 95% CI: 1.45–2.17). Both central and general obesity were independently associated with hypertension. Routine WC assessment alongside BMI may improve identification of high-risk individuals in India’s middle-aged and older population.

records.title: Incentives for Access: Changes in Admissions and Care Delivery for Metastatic Cancer Patients in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities, After the Patient-Driven Payment Model
records.abstract: Cancer patients experience suboptimal care in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs). Medicare’s Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) incentivized SNFs to admit complex patients, potentially promoting admissions without appropriate changes in care delivery.  To evaluate changes in SNF admissions, rehabilitation therapy volume, and chemotherapy/radiation around admission or discharge, following PDPM and COVID-19.  Adjusted interrupted time series examining 1,125,782 hospital stays from metastatic cancer patients, using 100% Traditional Medicare claims (2018–2021).  PDPM was associated with increased SNF admissions (0.47 pp/month; 95% CI: [0.17, 0.76]) and an immediate reduction in therapy volume (−24.95 minutes per day, 95% CI: [−26.40, −23.48]). Chemotherapy use remained low, but increased by 21% at PDPM implementation, without subsequent slope change (RR: 1.21; 95% CI: [1.01, 1.46]); radiation was unchanged. COVID-19 reversed admission gains. SNF admissions for metastatic cancer patients increased without sustained changes in cancer-relevant care delivery, warranting investigation of health outcomes and outcome-driven policy.

records.title: Social Engagement Programs of Area Agencies on Aging: Understanding Efforts to Reduce Social Isolation and Loneliness Among Older Adults
records.abstract: Social isolation and loneliness in later life are major public health concerns associated with increased morbidity and premature mortality. Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) constitute the primary local infrastructure for aging services in the US.  To describe social engagement program types and partnership structures among AAAs and to examine rural–non-rural differences.  We analyzed data from the 2025 National Survey of AAAs (n = 449). Descriptive statistics summarized program and partnership prevalence; item-level Pearson chi-square tests with Bonferroni adjustments compared rural and non-rural agencies.  Most AAAs offered multiple social engagement programs; volunteer engagement (66.0%), arts and creative activities (62.2%), visiting/calling programs (57.7%), and technology engagement (55.5%) were common. Non-rural AAAs were more likely to offer visiting/calling, technology-based activities, and memory cafes, while rural AAAs were more likely to partner with public health units. Rural–non-rural differences suggest context-specific influences of resources and infrastructure on program availability.

records.title: Structural Vulnerability and the Pandemic: Widening Gaps in Nursing Home Antipsychotic Prescribing
records.abstract: To assess whether national reductions in antipsychotic prescribing in U.S. nursing homes were shared equitably or masked widening gaps between top and bottom performers, we examined distributional trends across facilities from 2013 to 2023 using national facility-level data (CMS Provider Data Catalog; LTCFocus). We modeled long-stay antipsychotic measure performance using linear quantile mixed regression, assessed mobility across performance quartiles with transition matrices, and evaluated facility characteristics associated with trajectories. From 2013 to 2019, prescribing fell across all quantiles, with the steepest reductions among the worst performers, narrowing gaps with the best. After 2020, progress diverged: lower-performing facilities experienced sharp setbacks while top performers maintained gains. Mobility analyses showed entrenched disadvantage, with bottom-quartile facilities disproportionately likely to remain there. Higher Medicaid share predicted decline, whereas higher star ratings predicted improvement. The pandemic reversed earlier equity gains, amplifying structural disparities and exposing unequal capacity to sustain improvement.

records.title: Ambivalent return: Older adults’ homecoming after wartime displacement
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Little is known about how older adults experience their return home after wartime displacement, particularly when home and community are altered or remain insecure. This longitudinal qualitative study examined continuity and change across the displacement–return transition.  Twelve participants (aged 65–92), previously interviewed during displacement (T1), were re-interviewed after returning home (T2) using a qualitative descriptive approach with thematic analysis.  Three themes emerged: (1) the unsettled return, involving altered security, unfamiliarity within the home, and disrupted community life; (2) continuity of social relationships and activities after return; and (3) shifts in life perspective and self-perception. These themes describe the shared dimensions of post-return experience, whereas the complementary diachronic analysis examined how these dimensions changed and combined across T1 and T2. A diachronic analysis identified four return trajectories: functioning but incomplete; ambivalent or gradual return requiring active reorganization; return supported by communal and social continuity and use of personal resources; and ongoing erosion and unresolved damage. Discussion These findings demonstrate that return is not restoration but a reconfiguration of person-environment fit, place identity, belonging, and security in later life. For older adults, this transition involved rebuilding environmental familiarity, security, belonging, and agency rather than simply resuming pre-displacement life. The study highlights social infrastructure as critical for post-return adaptation, underscoring the need for policies recognizing the return process as a significant transition requiring continued communal support.

records.title: Transportation Use, Trip Taking, and Trip Purposes Among Older Adults Not in the Labor Force: Evidence From the 2022 National Household Travel Survey
records.abstract: Transportation needs may differ by labor-force participation status, yet little is known about travel behavior among older adults not in the labor force.  To examine alternative transportation use, trip taking, and trip purposes among older adults not in the labor force.  Data came from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey ( N = 3,474; aged ≥65; not in the labor force). Logistic regression models examined factors associated with transportation mode, taking any trip on the assigned reporting day, and trip purposes.  Nearly 87% drove, 5%–7% used rideshare/taxi, public transit, or bicycles, and one-third walked for transportation. Transportation use and trip-taking varied by socioeconomic characteristics, living arrangements, and digital engagement. Drivers, transportation walkers, and college graduates were more likely to travel. Social/recreational trips were more common among those living alone and among college graduates.  Improving transportation accessibility, affordability, and digital literacy may support late-life mobility and community participation.

records.title: Reducing Stress in Caregivers of People With Dementia in Psychiatric Care: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of an Emotion-Focused Group Intervention
records.abstract: Caregivers of people with dementia (CPwD) are at higher risk for psychological stress and mental health issues.  This study evaluated the effectiveness of a brief, four-session group intervention combining socio-medical education, mindfulness and emotion-focused support in reducing stress and improving psychological outcomes in an acute psychiatric hospital setting.  A within-subject waiting-period control design with repeated measures was conducted with N = 52 CPwD. Assessments were performed at baseline, pre-intervention, post-intervention and follow-up. Changes across phases were analyzed using subsequent contrast analyses.  Following the intervention, perceived stress decreased significantly ( p = .038) and general functioning improved ( p = .002) at follow-up. No significant changes were found for depressive symptoms or subjective well-being. The study protocol was designed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the joint Ethics Committee of the medical faculty at the Ludwig-Maximilians-University of Munich (project number 22-0995).

records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: In contemporary dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are often understood as expressions of the person's intentions or needs. This paper examines the limits of understanding BPSD as “expressions of intention” in severe Alzheimer's disease. It argues that while desires may still be preserved, the formation and maintenance of beliefs—an essential constituent of intentions in the standard desire–belief model—are likely to be severely compromised. As a result, many behavioral and perceptual symptoms closely related to basic activities of daily living cannot be adequately explained within an intention-based framework. As a complementary framework to existing dementia care theories, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of BPSD as arising from the interaction between embodied procedural memory and environmental affordances. Many BPSD are better understood not as expressions of intention, but as the outcome of situational and non-selective reactivation of fragments of relatively preserved procedural memory in response to the structure of the immediate environment. This reconceptualization extends the focus of care practice beyond the interpretation of the presumed meanings or intentions underlying BPSD and highlights the importance of modifying care environments in ways that appropriately support or constrain the reactivation of procedural memory.

records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: Ageism is widespread and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, with resource shortages contributing to healthcare guidelines that systematically deprioritised older adults. Whilst the ethical considerations of these guidelines are well documented, perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare allocation remain underexplored. This study examined younger and older adults’ perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare during COVID-19 through a social identity approach. Using a story completion method, 22 older and 41 younger adult participants completed a story about a younger or older COVID-19 patient and doctors allocating the last available ventilator. Using thematic analysis, three themes were developed: (1) age determines health, (2) age determines the value of life, and (3) age determines acceptance of death.  support the need for policies protecting against the influence of ageism in healthcare systems and emphasise the need to understand how internalised ageism may influence perceptions and health behaviours of older patients.

records.title: ‘Keeping me sharp”: Self-perceived effects of grandparenthood on cognition: An exploratory thematic analysis
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The experience of grandparenthood holds the potential for novel and engaging social interactions and activities, which may protect against cognitive decline. The present study outlines how individuals believe grandparenthood has impacted their cognitive abilities in late life.  We asked 127 grandparents (87 grandmothers and 40 grandfathers) how they thought grandparenthood had impacted their mental ability (memory, concentration, and cognitive ability). An exploratory thematic analysis utilizing a codebook approach was conducted on the participant responses.  Analysis revealed four major themes among the responses: “grandparenthood as a continuous experience that promotes healthy cognitive functioning”, “shifting perspectives”, “limited interaction”, and “the negative impacts of grandparenthood.” Discussion A majority of grandparents expressed the belief that interacting with their grandchildren is beneficial to their cognition. However, some participants qualified grandparenthood as a stressful experience that has negatively impacted their cognitive health. These findings support previous literature showing both cognitive benefits associated with grandparental caregiving and negative cognitive outcomes that may result from the stress of caregiving.

records.title: Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) and Cognition: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: To map the evidence of disparities in cognition across different social determinants of health (SDOH), examine how SDOH are measured in the context of research on cognitive outcomes and identify knowledge gaps. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched. We included peer-reviewed studies of adults that examined SDOH as primary exposures in relation to cognitive outcomes, and described a SDOH framework or definition in the context of cognition. Non-human studies, case reports, case series, editorials, protocols, and -only records were excluded. Ninety-one records were included. Most of the included studies were conducted in the US and the most frequently used framework was the Healthy People (2030) framework. Among studies examining a single SDOH indicator, the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) was the most used measure. Most of the existing research failed to explain the concept of SDOH and lacked a framework to guide the inclusion and interpretation of SDOH indicators. SDOH measures were heterogeneous across studies, with many examining only a single indicator and limited use of multidimensional approaches. This heterogeneity made findings challenging to compare. More research is needed on multidimensional SDOH and cognition in various racial/ethnic groups and less-studied geographic and cultural contexts, under explicit SDOH frameworks.

records.title: Control Beliefs and Emotional Aspects of Psychological Frailty Among Couples in Later Life
records.abstract: This study investigated the associations between control beliefs and the emotional aspects of psychological frailty (i.e., depression, anxiety, and loneliness) among older married couples.  Multivariate Actor-Partner Interdependence Models were used to analyze data from 538 couples aged 65 or older, drawn from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study.  Individuals’ own control beliefs were consistently associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, and loneliness for both spouses. A partner effect emerged for loneliness, with wives’ control beliefs associated with lower levels of loneliness in their husbands, but this was not significant after adjusting for marital support and strain. Discussion These findings identify control beliefs as a consistent individual-level protective factor. Interventions to improve emotional well-being in older couples should prioritize strengthening personal control beliefs. Dyadic processes merit further investigation, particularly for outcomes such as loneliness that are closely embedded in the relational context.

records.title: Latent Structures of Social Determinants of Health in Later Life: A Comparison of U.S.-Born and Immigrants
records.abstract: This study examined whether the latent structure of social determinants of health (SDOH) differs by nativity and how they relate to health outcomes in later life.  Using 2016–2018 HRS data, exploratory factor analyses by nativity were conducted, followed by nativity-stratified regressions linking SDOH factors to health outcomes.  Four comparable factors emerged in both groups: neighborhood environment, interpersonal stressors, socioeconomic resources, and family support. Loading patterns showed modest nativity differences: among immigrants, social isolation aligned more strongly with family support than socioeconomic resources and perceived discrimination loaded weakly on interpersonal stressors. Interpersonal stressors were associated with poorer mental and cognitive health in both groups; socioeconomic resources were associated with better health outcomes but more weakly among immigrants. Associations of neighborhood environment and family support with health varied by nativity. Discussion Findings indicate substantial commonality in SDOH structures alongside suggestive nativity-related differences, warranting replication in larger immigrant samples.

records.title: Does the Pilot Long-Term Care Insurance Work as Expected in China? Examining its Impact on Hospital Utilizations, Medical Expenses, and Health
records.abstract: This study investigates the impact of long-term care insurance (LTCI) on older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Using national representative data from four waves of CHARLS (2011, 2013, 2015, 2018), we find that LTCI decreases older adults’ monthly outpatient visits but is associated with an increase in both annual inpatient stays and inpatient medical expenses. Further evidence suggests that older adults covered by the pilot LTCI program have better health status compared to their counterparts in non-pilot cities. Overall, findings offer empirical support for the role of the LTCI program in Chinese older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Findings of China’s LTCI may offer insights for other countries with a large aging population but with no feasible LTCI framework.

records.title: Association Between a Hybrid Video-Guided Multicomponent Exercise Program With Staff Assistance and Free-Living Gait in Older Adults With Knee and Low Back Pain: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
records.abstract: Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as  indicators of mobility.  In this study, we aimed to examine the effects of a 12-week hybrid exercise-based program on daily-life walking characteristics.  A total of 59 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥65 years) with mild to moderate knee and/or low back pain were randomized to either a hybrid exercise group or an educational control group. Daily-life walking was monitored using an ankle sensor. Daily observation data were collected within 2 planned 7-day windows. Primary parameters included activity volume and gait characteristics. Statistical analyses were conducted based on a modified intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models, with a per-protocol set used for sensitivity analyses.  The mixed-effects analysis based on the modified intention-to-treat principle (n=52 participants; 696 observations) suggested an effect of the intervention on improving walking quality, particularly step length (β=2.39 cm; P =.04; Hedges g =0.493), with a smaller effect with borderline statistical significance observed on improving walking speed (β=0.05 m/s; P =.06; Hedges g =0.496). Cadence, daily distance, daily steps, active energy expenditure, and accumulated 3 or more metabolic equivalent of task activities showed no clear difference between the groups. In the per-protocol sensitivity analysis (n=44), the same directional pattern of improvement was observed for step length (β=1.95 cm; P =.13; Hedges g =0.365) and walking speed (β=0.04 m/s; P =.14; Hedges g =0.368); however, the estimates were imprecise.  A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.

records.title: Socioeconomic Differences in the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Episodic Memory Trajectories in Midlife and Old Age
records.abstract: : Episodic memory trajectories vary substantially between individuals in the second half of life: some maintain high levels of performance into their 80s, whereas others experience marked declines as early as their 50s. Identifying factors that help explain this heterogeneity is critical for understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on the resource substitution hypothesis and the Openness–Fluid–Crystallized–Intelligence (OFCI) model, this preregistered study examined whether the Big Five personality traits and their interactions with socioeconomic status (SES) predict individual differences in episodic memory trajectories, testing also potential non-linear associations. We expected higher openness and lower neuroticism to be associated with better memory levels and slower decline, with stronger effects at lower levels of SES. : We analyzed data from 57,947 individuals aged 50 and older (M = 67.78, SD = 9.03) who participated in at least two waves (7, 8, or 9) of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Multilevel growth models were used to estimate associations between personality and episodic memory levels and 5-year change, and whether SES (i.e., education, income, and wealth) moderated these associations. : Consistent with the OFCI model and the resource substitution hypothesis, higher openness was associated with better episodic memory levels, particularly among individuals with lower wealth. Higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness were linked to poorer episodic memory levels, but only among less wealthy individuals. Higher extraversion was associated with better memory levels overall, and individuals at the extremes of extraversion exhibited somewhat flatter declines compared to those with moderate levels. Except for extraversion, there was little evidence for non-linear associations or for associations with 5-year change in episodic memory. : Our findings underscore the relevance of wealth as an important socioeconomic resource for cognitive health beyond income and education, particularly in old age, when income is typically reduced. Overall, the  support modest concurrent associations between personality, SES, and episodic memory levels, but provide hardly any evidence for longitudinal effects. More frequent and longer-term longitudinal assessments are needed to clarify potential effects on cognitive aging.

records.title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study
records.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of  impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.  This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.  We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.  Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and F 1 -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns.  A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.

records.title: Blind giving predicts longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility in later life
records.abstract: and  Financial fraud is a common and consequential threat among older adults, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 4% to 17% annually. Although cognitive decline has been widely studied as a risk factor, less is known about behavioral characteristics that may predict changes in scam susceptibility. In the present study, we examined whether blind giving predicted trajectories of scam susceptibility across a two-year period and whether this association differed as a function of age. Research Design and  One hundred and sixteen cognitively unimpaired older adults (aged 51 to 83; 72% female) completed a behavioral economic measure of blind giving at baseline and a self-report measure of scam susceptibility annually across three visits.  Linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant interaction between time, blind giving, and age (p = .022), such that greater baseline blind giving was associated with increasing scam susceptibility over time among relatively older participants, whereas scam susceptibility remained stable across levels of blind giving among relatively younger participants. Blind giving was not associated with scam susceptibility at baseline (p = .515), and the longitudinal association persisted after separately adjusting for global cognition, socioeconomic status, and race (all ps ≤ .026).  Greater blind giving predicted longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility over a two-year period, with this pattern observed specifically in advanced age. These findings suggest that prosocial tendencies may become maladaptive in later life, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk individuals to inform prevention efforts in aging populations.

records.title: Heat stress and coping strategies among older adults in three Sunbelt cities in the United States
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Prevailing scientific evidence suggests that extreme heat poses a substantial threat to the health and well-being of older adults in the Sunbelt cities of the United States. However, prior research has not adequately addressed the specific socio-demographic, health-related vulnerabilities, and coping-strategic factors influencing heat stress among older urban populations.  Informed by the Socio-Ecological Model, this study adopts a retrospective cohort study design to investigate the predictors and experiences of heat stress among older adults. Data from older adults in Los Angeles, Houston, and Phoenix were analyzed using thematic and multiple binary logistic regression analyses.  The  reveal that much older adults (aged 80 +) were less likely to experience heat stress compared to their relatively younger counterparts. Also, marital status, income, respiratory diseases, physical activity, taking cool showers, and city of residence were significantly associated with a higher risk of suffering heat stress. The qualitative  uncovered individual-level behavioural adjustment as an effective coping mechanism during extreme heat events.  These  underscore the complex interplay of behavioral, socio-demographic, and health-related factors influencing heat stress among older adults. The study recommends that urban health strategies prioritize these demographics, enhancing support systems and coping mechanisms to reduce vulnerability to heat stress among older urban populations.

records.title: Being Sensed, Scored, and ‘Connected’: A Social-Gerontological Critique of AI-Driven Loneliness Detection for Older Adults in Taiwan
records.abstract: Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) that continuously infers emotion promises to change how care systems identify older adults at risk of loneliness. We use AI-driven loneliness detection to mean systems that infer loneliness, or a proxy for it, from sensed data rather than from a person’s answer, rendering the inference as a score or category used in care; they range from facial and vocal emotion recognition to behavioral risk prediction from everyday activity data. Engineering feasibility, more than any social-gerontological understanding of loneliness, has driven this agenda, and little attention has gone to how older adults in different cultural contexts wish to be known and supported. Because such detection is not yet in routine use in Taiwan, this Forum article adopts an anticipatory-governance stance, examining before deployment a trajectory that policy makes plausible. Anchored in Taiwan’s ageing society and long-term care system, it argues that culturally responsive design should begin with older adults’ own meanings, relational obligations, and expectations of privacy and autonomy, not with the sensors. It identifies three tensions for social gerontology: the reframing of a relational experience as an individual biometric deficit; the risk that algorithms read culturally patterned emotional restraint as noise; and the slippage from care toward surveillance once risk indices enter routine care workflows. Taking seriously the case for technological augmentation of scarce care resources, the article proposes principles for a socially accountable approach and a research agenda on how older adults negotiate being sensed, scored, and ‘connected.’

records.title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort
records.abstract: Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.  This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.  This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.  At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.  Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.
